feed.title: Cryptography & Security · Diting Lab
feed.subtitle: Research papers and global crypto regulation, at a glance
feed.rights: Explanations and summaries are generated by AI from the original text. Dates, rates and amounts are checked against the source, but errors are still possible, so always rely on the original. Nothing here is legal, tax or investment advice.

entry.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates for Stronger Prompt Injection Defense
entry.summary: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper introduces Heads of Security (HoS), a defense against prompt injection that uses a small set of learned attention gates in each attention head to separate instructions from untrusted data. The gates learn how attention should be divided between trusted and untrusted tokens, so models can process untrusted content without following injected instructions. Tested on Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B, HoS shows greater robustness to adaptive attacks and better utility than SecAlign++ and ASIDE, and matches top results on agentic benchmarks.

entry.title: Classical verification of quantum computation beyond the polynomial hierarchy
entry.summary: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 The paper studies whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can check arbitrary quantum polynomial-time computations without computational assumptions. Relative to a classical oracle, it constructs a language outside the polynomial hierarchy that is exactly decidable in quantum polynomial time, with a public-coin protocol having perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. The message count is shown to be optimal up to a constant factor. ★★★★ Notable: Constructs an oracle-relative language beyond the polynomial hierarchy with a perfectly complete public-coin proof system, using a new switching theorem for correlated restrictions; novel and rigorous

entry.title: Privacy risks of quantized neural networks: do compressed models leak more training data?
entry.summary: Revisiting Privacy Risks in Quantized Deep Neural Networks arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper presents the first comprehensive empirical study of privacy risks in quantized deep neural networks, evaluating eight membership inference attacks across six quantization methods. Practical quantization levels of 4 to 8 bits have limited effect on membership privacy, leaving quantized models about as vulnerable as full-precision ones. Aggressive 2-bit quantization yields some privacy gains but substantially degrades utility. Existing defenses designed for full-precision models offer limited protection for quantized models while further amplifying utility loss.

entry.title: When POST Becomes GET: How Interchangeable HTTP Methods Can Create Security Gaps
entry.summary: When POST Becomes GET: Investigating HTTP Method Interchangeability and Its Security Implications arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper studies HTTP method interchangeability, where a POST request to an endpoint is rewritten as a GET request with its body parameters moved into the query string, yielding an equivalent response. The authors present MIDE, an automated pipeline that crawls web applications, converts captured POST requests, and compares responses. In an unauthenticated experiment on the Tranco top 10k, they found high-confidence interchangeable requests on 407 sites. The study also reports CSRF token-replay cases and conditions related to Web Cache Deception.

entry.title: "Penny for Your Prompts": A Study of Chat Data Leaks on AI Platforms
entry.summary: Penny for Your Prompts: A Measurement Study of Contextual Leakage in AI Chat Platforms arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 This paper measures how 42 AI chatbot web interfaces, including general-purpose and health, legal, and education platforms, share data with third parties. The researchers instrumented the browser's JavaScript engine to trace each data flow back to the user action that triggered it. They found that 21 platforms leak conversation titles and nine leak verbatim user prompts to third-party trackers, and many also send users' emails.

entry.title: SecDMP: A Provably Secure Data Prefetcher Defense (Extended Version)
entry.summary: SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching (Extended Version) arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 Data memory-dependent prefetchers (DMPs) are a CPU optimization in recent mainstream processors that can improve performance but may leak secrets through side channels. The paper classifies DMP leakage, categorizes existing and new attacks, and validates the analysis by implementing open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor. It proposes SecDMP, a hardware defense in which secrets are marked in memory so DMPs never encode them in the microarchitecture. The authors formally prove SecDMP adds no leakage beyond a baseline without DMPs. ★★★★★ Notable: Classifies DMP leakage and proposes SecDMP, a formally proven hardware defense blocking all leakage classes while preserving public-data performance.

entry.title: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Defense Surface for LLM Agents
entry.summary: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Surface of LLM Agent Defense arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 The paper builds on prior work that treats the envelope layer as the channel through which malicious content enters an agent. Using the A2A-TIBA attack as a test vehicle, it runs a two-by-two factorial experiment and a memory experiment to examine how label strength, envelope authenticity, scaffold differences, and existing memories affect defense. Strong labels reduce semantic breach rates when envelopes are authentic, but weak labels are not always better than no label, and strong labels lose effect when envelopes can be forged. Memory has a larger effect than label manipulation. The authors refine the envelope layer into an admission channel and a context assembly surface, arguing its security boundary depends on label claims, frontend permissions, and historical memory together.

entry.title: Commit-boundary authorization guardrail for AI agents resolving entity identities
entry.summary: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution arXiv · Oct 28, 2026 The paper proposes an authorization boundary for agentic entity resolution systems that separates evidence usable for reasoning from evidence allowed to authorize persistent identity changes. A domain-governed function maps reconstruction failures to identity-preserving constraints, and a two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when evidence covers every required proposition, conflicts are resolved, the operation is in scope, and versions are valid. It is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation.

entry.title: Watermark Basins: Detecting Distilled LLMs Using Only API Access
entry.summary: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper addresses API-based distillation, where an adversary trains a student model on a proprietary teacher model's outputs, and how providers can watermark outputs to detect it. The authors find that watermarked training creates a persistent, key-specific geometric signal in parameter space, orthogonal to ordinary fine-tuning directions. They propose WM-Basin, a black-box detector that needs only API queries, and report that it outperforms a token-level baseline on mathematical reasoning distillation while the signal survives quantization, pruning, and reinforcement-learning post-training. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a watermark basin signal orthogonal to task subspaces, detected via gradient alignment; evaluated across 135M to 8.2B students with clear gains over the token-level baseline.

entry.title: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs and the Trust Trap in Graph Learning
entry.summary: When Is a Relation Worth Trusting? Manipulation Costs, Exposure, and the Trust Trap in Multi-Relational Graph Learning arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper studies multi-relational graph detectors, which learn how much to trust each relation from clean data, while attackers face different manipulation costs per relation. It proves that degree gating beats any selection or reweighting of a relation when part of the population is isolated on it and the attacker cannot afford to open the gate. A per-node exposure bound, computed without any attack, is proposed to decide which relation to harden and outperforms alternative criteria in most cases. Without cost information, the authors conclude the safe choice is to abstain from using the graph. ★★★★ Notable: Proves degree gating strictly beats relation selection under sharp conditions, with real-graph validation and exact worst-case bounds; impact is confined to graph-security subfield.

entry.title: Asynchronous Verifiable and Complete Secret Sharing: Design Patterns and System Trade-offs
entry.summary: Asynchronous Verifiable and Complete Secret Sharing: From Design Patterns to System-Level Trade-offs arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper examines secret sharing protocols that aim to work in fully asynchronous systems with Byzantine faults, where practical costs are hard to compare across studies. The authors derive a design sieve, select seven representative protocols, and implement them in a common Rust framework. Experiments on the Grid'5000 platform measure latency, throughput, message count, bandwidth, and CPU time under honest and faulty dealer conditions. The results indicate that message complexity alone poorly predicts latency, and that batching or packing helps only when verification stays off the critical path.

entry.title: GKS Fully Homomorphic Encryption: A Security Analysis
entry.summary: GKS Fully Homomorphic Encryption: Security Analysis arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper gives a formal security analysis of the Gribov-Kahrobaei-Shpilrain (GKS) private-key fully homomorphic encryption scheme. Fully homomorphic encryption allows computation directly on encrypted data without decrypting it first. The paper states that GKS requires no bootstrapping or de-linearization, produces bit-exact decryption, supports native encrypted search, and scales to unbounded depth.

entry.title: Janus Vehicles: A Threat Model for Authentic Cars That Secretly Misbehave
entry.summary: Janus Vehicles: Entity-Centric Threat Modelling of Protocol-Conformant Vehicles under a Malicious-Manufacturer Assumption arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper challenges the automotive security assumption that manufacturers are benign, focusing on vehicles that are authentic and protocol-conformant yet perform undeclared sensing, communication, or triggered actions. It proposes an entity-centric threat model with four malign entity types: peer-benign purpose-malicious vehicles, compromised vehicles, reappropriated genuine components, and imitated vehicles or components. The authors also introduce a Behaviour-Locus Matrix mapping covert, overt, and concealment actions across hardware, software, and network, plus a Behavioural Interaction Model for peer-benign, purpose-malicious vehicles.

entry.title: Blindfold: Keeping Random Audit Checks Hidden from LLM Agents
entry.summary: Blindfold: Keeping the Audit Coin Secret from LLM Agents arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies audit-based certification, which limits an LLM agent's violation rate by auditing a random fraction of its actions and reweighting the results. The authors show that validity also requires the audit coin to stay hidden from the agent before its action is committed. They define this as pre-commit noninterference, measure it, and derive bounds on the resulting bias. Experiments on a monitor and a real LLM agent show that a visible audit notice leaks the coin and breaks the certificate, while a silent audit or a fresh coin per audited call restores validity. ★★★★ Notable: Introduces pre-commit noninterference with tight bias bounds, a novel theory; experiments on LLM agents confirm the channel but at limited scale.

entry.title: RePAIR: Reversing Backdoor Attacks in Semantic Segmentation
entry.summary: RePAIR: Inverting Backdoor Attacks in Semantic Segmentation arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents RePAIR, a post-hoc, label-free defense against backdoor attacks on semantic segmentation models that does not depend on knowing the attack method. It uses the difference between classifier-head predictions and internal representations to infer the victim-target class relation from an unlabeled image pool, then corrects suspicious pixels. Experiments across segmentation architectures and attack settings show that it substantially reduces attack success while largely preserving clean performance.

entry.title: Distributed log parsing: how many clients affect results, and how to measure them.
entry.summary: Too many clients spoil the logs: distributed parsing, aggregation techniques and metrics arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies log parsing in distributed settings for anomaly detection in IoT systems, where several organizations must agree on log templates. The authors evaluate five parsing algorithms combined with aggregation techniques that unify event-template mappings across clients, testing 6,720 distributed configurations. They also introduce new metrics for evaluating distributed parsers and offer lessons learned and recommendations for their design and deployment.

entry.title: A dynamic multi-factor authentication system to secure smart organizations
entry.summary: Developing a Dynamic Multi-factor Authentication System for Securing Smart Organizations arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper proposes a dynamic multi-factor authentication system within a Zero Trust Architecture that enforces continuous verification. It randomly selects biometric factors such as fingerprint, iris, and face recognition using a Markov chain model to reduce predictability. Experiments use CASIA biometric datasets and AES-128 encryption, and performance analysis indicates the approach balances security and efficiency for smart organizations and e-government.

entry.title: Alg{Ossa}: Decentralized Secure Aggregation with Rotating Committees and Eventual Delivery
entry.summary: Alg\Ossa\: Decentralized Secure Aggregation with Rotating Committees and Eventual Delivery IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents Ossa, a generic secure aggregation construction for one-shot clients using a single server and committee assistance, where a malicious server learns only the aggregate. It integrates Ossa into an Algorand-style consensus backbone, using cryptographic sortition to select leaders and committees each round. The authors prove a positive lower bound on the probability that the selected server is honest, yielding eventual delivery of a non-empty aggregate across repeated rounds. Complete classical rounds are evaluated, and feasibility of a post-quantum instantiation is demonstrated.

entry.title: HqcLethe: streaming HQC key encapsulation for tiny stateless servers
entry.summary: HqcLethe: Streaming HQC Encapsulation for Tiny Stateless Servers arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents HqcLethe, a stateless post-quantum key exchange that streams an HQC key encapsulation in packet-sized pieces, so servers need not buffer multi-packet handshakes and avoid memory-exhaustion attacks. It uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split polynomial multiplication into independent, masked remainders, one per packet. The authors prove in Rocq with SSProve that the masked pieces reveal no more than an ordinary HQC ciphertext, and verify session secrecy, server authentication and forward secrecy in ProVerif. On a Raspberry Pi 3B+, each worker uses a fixed 1.2-1.6 MiB, and at category 5 it sends 27x fewer bytes and uses 9.0x less server CPU than McTiny. ★★★★ Notable: Uses the Chinese remainder theorem to split HQC polynomial multiplication into independent packet pieces, with formal proofs and protocol verification.

entry.title: The Content Leash: Reducing Degenerate Solutions in Reversible Speaker Anonymization
entry.summary: The Content Leash: Mitigating Degenerate Solutions in Invertible Speaker Anonymization arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies reversible voice anonymization, which hides a speaker's identity while keeping the spoken content, and lets authorized users recover the original voice. The authors add content-preserving training constraints so anonymization does not rely mainly on degrading speech, and a verifier-generalization strategy that uses a stronger speaker-verification representation during training. On 38 unseen speakers, the attacker's equal error rate rises from 2.8% to 26.3%, and to 27.9% against a held-out verifier. Key-based restoration yields an 11.8% word error rate and 94.9% speaker similarity.

entry.title: Breaking Fisher-Yates Shuffling: Recovering Length-128 Permutations for ML-DSA Side-Channel Attacks
entry.summary: Unshuffling Fisher-Yates: Practical Recovery of Length-128 Permutations and Application to ML-DSA IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies side-channel attacks on shuffled number-theoretic transforms in ML-DSA, a lattice-based post-quantum signature scheme. The authors recover a length-128 permutation generated by Fisher-Yates from a single trace, using timing and Hamming weight leakage, modeled as a constraint-programming problem. They show that the recovered permutations allow secret polynomial s1 to be recovered, so Fisher-Yates shuffling alone does not prevent key recovery.

entry.title: Poly2MsgLeaks: Certified Key Recovery via Polynomial-to-Message Power Leakage
entry.summary: Poly2MsgLeaks: Certified Key Recovery from Polynomial-to-Message Leakage IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents Poly2MsgLeaks, a profiled chosen-ciphertext power-analysis attack that recovers the full 512-coefficient secret key of the SMAUG-T public-key encryption scheme in its TiMER parameter set. Using six physical polynomial-to-message traces recorded on an STM32F415, the attack recovers 999 of 1,000 unseen secrets, and recovers all 1,000 secrets of a second cohort at a mean cost of 7.021 traces without false acceptances. Against single-write message assembly and a two-share masked P2M implementation, the evaluated six-execution attack recovers no complete secret.

entry.title: Post-quantum assumptions if the Dihedral Coset Problem is broken
entry.summary: Beyond LWE: Post-Quantum Assumptions under a Counterfactual Break of the Dihedral Coset Problem arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This survey examines the consequences of a genuine breakthrough on the Dihedral Coset Problem, motivated by a refuted 2026 claim of an efficient quantum algorithm for it. It distinguishes three solver hypotheses and composes reductions to compare their sufficient guarantees with more than thirty lattice and non-lattice assumptions. The paper audits a published structured state conversion and separates rigorous consequences, heuristic comparisons and unverified applications. It closes with open questions and a scenario-planning checklist.

entry.title: Recovering Falcon Private Keys by Combining Sampler Side-Channel Leakages
entry.summary: Falcon Key Recovery from Joint Sampler Leakages IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 Falcon and the FN-DSA standard based on it create signatures using discrete Gaussian sampling, and power consumption during this step leaks information about secret-dependent values. The paper presents a key-recovery method that combines three observations from each sampler call and turns the resulting candidate sets into constraints on the secret key, solved by regression and integer reconstruction without lattice reduction like LLL or BKZ. The attack recovers all 50 evaluation keys on PQClean Falcon-512 and still recovers 38 of 50 keys on c-fn-dsa, showing that instruction-level normalization alone is insufficient.

entry.title: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Agent for Auditing Privacy Leaks in LLM Jailbreak Responses
entry.summary: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent for Auditing Privacy Leakage in LLM Jailbreak Responses arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper addresses the difficulty of reliably judging whether jailbreak responses from large language models reveal personal information, especially when disclosures are indirect or obfuscated. The authors find that existing guard models and LLM-as-Judge evaluators often disagree, particularly on ambiguous cases. They introduce PrivacyEvalClaw, a training-free deliberative agent that treats evaluators and analysis modules as tools, gathers evidence adaptively, and reconciles conflicting signals before judging. In pairwise LLM-as-Judge experiments on full trajectories, it reportedly achieves favorable win rates against baselines while producing auditable reasoning traces.[ok]

entry.title: Measuring and ranking stealthy source-manipulation threats to multi-source anomaly detectors
entry.summary: Quantifying and Prioritizing Stealthy Source-Manipulation Threats Against Multi-Source Anomaly Detectors arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper studies how an adversary controlling some data sources can stealthily manipulate a downstream decision in a multi-source security pipeline. The authors propose a task-conditioned visibility margin, the least detector evidence a manipulation must reveal per unit of harm to the downstream task, which has a closed form and yields minimum-evidence attacks. On a 17-channel industrial telemetry benchmark, a detector flagging 82.8% of random single-channel corruptions was first-order blind on 64.7% of task/subset pairs across one- to four-channel audits.

entry.title: Does speed compromise safety? Safer few-step text-to-image models
entry.summary: Haste Makes Waste? Towards Safe Few-Step Text-to-Image Models arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 Few-step distilled text-to-image models are attractive for their fast generation, but their rate of unsafe outputs was unknown. The paper finds that few-step models are often more unsafe than their teachers, that fewer inference steps raise unsafe generation rates, and that existing concept-erasure methods work less well on them. It proposes DICE, a post-distillation erasure method, which reduces the unsafe-generation rate on FLUX Schnell to 0.046 while mostly preserving benign generation quality.

entry.title: OblivDGL: A Practical Privacy-Preserving Deep Graph Learning Framework
entry.summary: OblivDGL: Oblivious Deep Graph Learning Made Practical IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents OblivDGL, a framework for secure graph neural network (GNN) inference and training that protects both graph data and models. Inspired by the Deep Graph Library (DGL), it introduces an oblivious message passing paradigm and an encrypted graph representation built on function secret sharing (FSS). According to the authors' evaluations on four benchmark graph datasets, OblivDGL cuts communication cost by up to 1024x and speeds up secure training by up to 14.3x compared with prior secure GNN frameworks, while inference achieves up to 754x lower communication and a 4.19x speedup.

entry.title: Measuring User Security and Privacy Concerns About Discord Third-Party Bots
entry.summary: Measuring Users' Security and Privacy Concerns About Third-Party Community Bots on Discord arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper analyzes 23,102 third-party Discord bots and 183,142 user reviews from 2021 to 2026. Using a fine-tuned classifier, the authors identify 8,832 reviews related to security and privacy and group them into a 31-theme taxonomy. The most common concerns involve data sharing and data collection. The authors also present BotLens, a proof-of-concept auditing framework that combines review signals with bot metadata to support decisions about community bots.

entry.title: Silent Blindness: Hardware Malware Detectors' Vulnerability to Faults
entry.summary: Silent Blindness: Fault Vulnerability of Hardware Malware Detectors arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies how faults in hardware malware detectors (HMDs), which classify performance-counter data, can weaken detection. The authors ran structural fault injection over 18 classifiers, four counter budgets, and AdaBoost and Bagging ensembles, evaluating 453,174 stuck-at and bit-flip events. Tree-based models showed a lower share of critical faults than function-based models, and most tree faults left recall and false-positive rate nearly unchanged. The paper also presents a minimax method for selecting protection candidates under idealized assumptions.

entry.title: Peak-DNA: Recurring Shape Patterns in Global Narrative Spread
entry.summary: Peak-DNA: Recurrent Morphology in Global Narrative Propagation arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents Peak-DNA, a framework for finding recurring propagation shapes in global news narrative streams. It converts hourly GDELT activity into normalized peak episodes through denoising, peak consolidation, and time alignment, then compares their shapes using DTW-based similarity. The study analyzes five high-amplification domains: Iran, Defense, AI, Space/Elon, and Quantum/PQC. Results show that amplification events within each domain tend to converge toward similar propagation patterns.

entry.title: CASEL: A runtime layer that decides how carefully AI tool calls should be checked before running
entry.summary: CASEL: Consequence-Aware Selective Execution for Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper introduces CASEL, a model-agnostic policy that chooses, for each tool call an AI agent proposes, whether to execute directly, verify, sandbox, clarify, seek approval, or abstain, based on failure probability, consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness. In a controlled simulation over 20 seeds with 120,000 test actions each, CASEL reduced harmful-side-effect trajectories from 14.75% to 7.02% compared with an uncertainty-ranked gate. The authors state that intervention effectiveness was assumed rather than measured, so the results rank allocation rules under simulator assumptions and do not establish deployment effectiveness.

entry.title: Algebraic structure and too many hints: rethinking side-channel leakage evaluation
entry.summary: When Algebraic Structure Meets Too Many Hints IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 The paper argues that DDGR hint classes and too-many-hints thresholds cannot serve as standalone security metrics for real side-channel leakage, because they ignore the algebraic structure of hint vectors. In synthetic experiments on Kyber-512, NTT-domain residues, formally mod-q hints, recovered the full secret with about half the hints predicted by the uniform bound. Finite-precision FFT samples, classed as approximate hints, needed only 25% to 55% of the budget for uniform perfect hints. Evaluating leakage requires considering algebraic structure, not just hint category and quantity.

entry.title: Split Federated Unlearning: Removing Learned Contributions from Partitioned Federated Learning
entry.summary: Split Federated Unlearning arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 Split federated learning combines partitioned model execution with federated aggregation for collaborative learning across distributed environments. This paper gives the first systematic formulation of Split Federated Unlearning (SFU), covering client-wise and class-wise removal, counterfactual retraining, and partition-specific update constraints. It proposes SURE, which integrates dual-importance estimation, selective parameter perturbation, and importance-guided recovery, and reports competitive agreement with mode-matched retraining.

entry.title: A concise introduction to robust membership inference attacks
entry.summary: A Simple Presentation of Robust Membership Inference Attacks arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 A membership inference attack lets an attacker, given one individual's data, guess whether that person was part of a dataset, using statistics from the dataset or a model trained on it. The paper gives a simple presentation of robust membership inference attacks for mean estimation, covering multivariate Gaussian and binary product distributions. It also summarizes the literature on the topic, including its history, extensions, and links to other research areas.

entry.title: No Tokenizer, Still a Gap: Fairness of Lookalike-Character Watermarks Across Languages
entry.summary: No Tokenizer, Still a Gap: Cross-Lingual Fairness of Homoglyph and Invisible-Character Watermarking arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies watermarks that hide signals by swapping characters for visually similar homoglyphs or inserting invisible characters after text is written, without involving the generating model. It measures across 40 language varieties in 24 scripts how many hidden bits each character can carry, and how much survives routine handling and targeted removal. Capacity varies 3.3-fold, with script accounting for 96% of the variation. Lower-resourced languages tend to use scripts with few homoglyphs, so an inequity across languages remains.

entry.title: What Victims Take Away: Reuse of Prompt-Injection Attacks and Defense Changes
entry.summary: What Victims Take Away: Attack Reuse and Defense Revision after Prompt-Injection Attacks arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies how players targeted by prompt-injection attacks in the online game Tensor Trust use the attack texts they received, using 563,349 attack records. Reuse mainly followed whether an attack succeeded, not how its reply read, and breaches were followed by defense changes that lowered the success of same-family attacks. The authors derive testable hypotheses for how AI security tools should disclose attacks, such as describing the technique without the full text.

entry.title: ORBITAL: Robust, Hardware-Efficient Compression for Brain-Computer Interface Decoders
entry.summary: ORBITAL: Optimization of Robust Brain--Computer Inference Through Architecture-Aware Low-Precision Compression arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents ORBITAL, a framework for compressing compact EEG decoders for brain-computer interfaces while preserving adversarial robustness and improving hardware efficiency. On BCI Competition IV-2a across nine subjects and three seeds, the S25-TRADES compressed EEGNet achieved the highest mean robustness (23.06% versus 21.27% for the standard full model), with 26.27% fewer parameters and 25.10% fewer MACs. On a Jetson Orin Nano, FP16 compression reduced board energy by up to 16.20% and latency by 8.00%, whereas native INT8 Q/DQ incurred about twice the FP16 latency and energy.

entry.title: Privacy-Aware Federated Vision-Language Models for Breast Cancer Imaging Evaluation
entry.summary: Evaluating Federated Vision-Language and Vision-Only Models for Privacy-Aware Breast Cancer Imaging arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper evaluates a federated learning framework that combines pretrained vision-language and vision-only models with client-level differential privacy for breast imaging. Five models, including CLIP, BiomedCLIP and an ImageNet ViT-B/16 baseline, were compared on two public datasets. Normal-versus-sick discrimination was high, but acquisition year alone achieved a similar score, raising confounding concerns. Benign-versus-malignant discrimination was uncertain, removing the text pathway halved communication cost while preserving accuracy, and differential privacy substantially reduced ROC-AUC.

entry.title: PHP2Shell and AI-Discovered Vulnerability Disclosure: Evidence, Verification, and Human Authority
entry.summary: PHP2Shell and the Future of AI-Discovered Vulnerability Disclosure: Evidence, Verification, and Human Authority arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper presents FedTrust-CVDv2, a federated framework for coordinated vulnerability disclosure that separates evidence validation, inter-organizational coordination, human governance, and permissioned auditing. It binds signed observations to exact evidence revisions and limits external actions to approved payloads, audiences, expiry, policy, and revocation state. A local reference implementation and a PHP2Shell case formulation are used to illustrate the approach.

entry.title: Detecting and Mitigating Query-Based System Prompt Leakage Attacks
entry.summary: Detecting and Mitigating Query-Based System Prompt Leakage Attacks arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents AdvGuard, a model-agnostic framework that detects and mitigates leakage of LLM system prompts through query-based attacks. Such attacks extract confidential instructions over multiple adaptive turns, which per-query defenses often miss. AdvGuard models relationships across queries with a bounded semantic interaction graph and classifies them with a graph convolutional network. It improves recall by up to 36% over the strongest baseline with a false positive rate of at most 3.4%, and substantially reduces prompt leakage in evaluated attack loops.

entry.title: BUSTA: Training Small Language Models to Reason About Binary Execution
entry.summary: BUSTA: Teaching Small Language Models to Reason About Binary Execution arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper examines whether targeted training can give small open language models reverse engineering skills. Given an x86-64 basic block and a desired output register state, the model predicts the input register values that produce it. After fine-tuning with GRPO, Qwen3-1.7B improves from 73.2% to 85.3% and Nemotron-3-Nano from 63.3% to 95.2% on knowable-register prediction. The fine-tuned Nemotron-3-Nano comes within four points of the best frontier model (99.2%) at a much smaller parameter count. The authors release both fine-tuned models and the training dataset.

entry.title: CTGREP: Finding Compiler-Induced Timing Leaks in Crypto Code at Scale
entry.summary: Analyzing Compiler-induced Constant-time Violations with Compiler at Scale IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper presents CTGREP, a compiler-based framework that uses differential analysis across the whole compilation chain to find where compilers break constant-time cryptographic code, how the violation is introduced, and which configurations cause it. The authors applied it to seven complete cryptographic libraries across three Clang versions, six platforms, and thousands of compiler configurations. They worked with library developers to fix 48 cases and identified seven new problematic LLVM passes. ★★★★ Notable: Differential analysis across the whole compilation chain improves on single-point detection; validated on seven crypto libraries, with 48 fixes and seven newly identified problematic LLVM passes.

entry.title: A method for choosing clipping bounds privately on heavy-tailed data
entry.summary: Privately Clipping Heavy-Tailed Data arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies vector summation in differentially private data analysis. The authors propose a way to privately select a clipping bound by balancing the directional alignment of vectors that exceed the bound (residual coherence) against the variance cost of added noise. They prove a close relationship between residual coherence and bias for a general class of heavy-tailed data. Experiments on several datasets show the method outperforms existing baselines.

entry.title: SpecGuard: Detecting Multi-Turn LLM Jailbreaks with Specification-Based Runtime Monitoring
entry.summary: SpecGuard: Detecting Multi-Turn LLM Jailbreaks via Specification-Based Runtime Monitoring arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper presents SpecGuard, a training-free framework that monitors multi-turn conversations with large language models using formal specifications written in Linear Temporal Logic. Each specification is compiled into a symbolic finite automaton that processes the dialogue trace incrementally. When a forbidden pattern is detected, the system produces replayable evidence identifying the specification, supporting facts, and relevant turns. Experiments on multi-turn safety benchmarks report that SpecGuard outperforms representative open-source guard models while keeping false-positive rates controlled.

entry.title: Reverse Substitution in Secret Sharing: Critical Threshold and Route to Superpolynomial Lower Bounds
entry.summary: Reverse Substitution in Secret Sharing: The Critical One-Half Threshold and a Route to Superpolynomial Lower Bounds IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies substitution, a way of building composite access structures by replacing one participant of an outer structure with an inner structure in secret sharing. It asks whether the contribution vector of any scheme for the composite structure can be reverse-factored into vectors for the outer and inner factors. The authors show exact reversal fails via a counterexample with factor 8/9, but prove a factor of 1/2 is always attainable. For a recursive family built from Csirmaz's access structure, they identify a critical factor slightly above one half whose crossing yields superlinear lower bounds, and show Shannon inequalities alone cannot reach it. ★★★★★ Notable: Introduces reverse substitution with a counterexample and a one-half threshold, offering a route to superpolynomial lower bounds; rigorous and potentially highly influential.

entry.title: Teaching hardware security within existing core courses so every student can learn it
entry.summary: Bringing Hardware Security Education to All: A Seamless Curriculum Integration Approach arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 The paper argues that undergraduate curricula largely overlook hardware security, and that dedicated courses reach very few students. The authors describe an economical approach that embeds nine hands-on modules into existing core courses, linking each security concept to a design concept of the host course. Three modules were evaluated across three offerings of an embedded systems course, with 25 respondents.

entry.title: "They Will See Johnny's Message": A Measurement Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography in Email Delivery
entry.summary: They Will See Johnny's Message: A Measurement Study of Post-Quantum Cryptography Across Email Delivery Paths arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper systematically measures post-quantum cryptography (PQC) deployment across email delivery stages, including relay, submission, and access services, as well as sending servers and OpenPGP and S/MIME implementations. It finds that PQC support is concentrated among a few providers and that available capability is not consistently used in practice. Usable PQC message encryption is further limited by key generation, key-format, and backend integration issues. ★★★★ Notable: Systematic multi-stage email PQC measurement reveals capability-use gaps and plaintext fallback, with strong evidence and significant impact on email security.

entry.title: HELLO, GOODBYE: Concurrent Composition with Fewer Extra Rounds
entry.summary: HELLO, GOODBYE: Concurrent General Composition From Super-Rushing Security IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies how to keep synchronous multiparty computation protocols secure when many executions run concurrently. Earlier methods added a synchronisation step after every round, roughly doubling the round count. The authors show that for protocols secure against super-rushing adversaries, adding only a start round (HELLO) and an end round (GOODBYE) suffices, giving security with selective abort in R+2 rounds. Using a broadcast channel for the end round upgrades the guarantee to unanimous abort. ★★★★★ Notable: Reduces concurrent general composition overhead from doubling rounds to adding two, with rigorous security reductions improving Kushilevitz-Lindell-Rabin.

entry.title: Log-To-Leak: Prompt injection attacks on tool-using LLM agents via the Model Context Protocol
entry.summary: Log-To-Leak: Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents via the Model Context Protocol arXiv · Oct 27, 2026 This paper studies security risks for LLM agents that access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It introduces Log-To-Leak, an attack that makes an agent place an extra, attacker-controlled tool call after the legitimate one, leaking the user query, server name, server response, and agent response. Across 18 valid model-server pairs, the attack reaches an attack success rate of 62.64% to 100%, and three tested defenses still leave over 55% residual success on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o. The authors conclude that a task can finish correctly while unauthorized disclosure happens, and they recommend host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls.} ★★★★ Notable: Proposes an additive post-hoc logging exfiltration attack on MCP tool poisoning, backed by multi-model, multi-server experiments and defense evaluations.
